title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
subtitle: The agreement that opened the door to war
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: A public promise of peace. A secret division of eastern Europe. How Germany and the Soviet Union reached their bargain—and what it meant for the countries between them.
body:
In Moscow on 23 August 1939, the foreign minister of Nazi Germany negotiated with the government his regime had spent years describing as an enemy. Joachim von Ribbentrop had come with Adolf Hitler’s authority to conclude an agreement quickly. Across the table stood Vyacheslav Molotov, the Soviet foreign commissar, and Joseph Stalin, whose approval would decide the outcome. Between them lay the future of countries whose governments had no place in the room.

The documents that emerged from the visit promised peace between Germany and the Soviet Union and contemplated the rearrangement of eastern Europe. One agreement would be announced to the world. The other would remain secret. Together, they transformed the strategic position of Poland, already facing German demands and preparations for invasion. [1] [2] The familiar date requires a small qualification. The treaty bore the date **23 August**, but negotiations and signing extended into the early hours of 24 August. Reporting from Moscow that morning, the American ambassador, Laurence Steinhardt, said the signatures had been affixed in the Kremlin with Stalin present. The historical date commemorates the agreement as dated by its makers; the diplomacy continued through the night. [3] Nine days after the treaty’s official date, Germany invaded Poland. The pact helped make that decision easier for Hitler. Its origins, however, reach back beyond the immediate crisis, to a European order built from the wreckage of one war and steadily undermined on the way to another.

An unsettled Europe

Poland recovered its independence in 1918 after more than a century of partition. Its reappearance accompanied the collapse of the empires that had ruled much of central and eastern Europe. Independence did not immediately provide settled frontiers. The Polish–Soviet conflict and the Treaty of Riga, signed on 18 March 1921, helped determine the eastern boundary of the restored state. That frontier survived until the upheaval of 1939. [4] The eastern provinces contained Polish, Ukrainian, Belarusian and Jewish communities, among others. Languages, religions and political loyalties crossed the lines on diplomatic maps. Poland’s neighbours disputed aspects of the settlement, and its internal nationalities question remained difficult. None of that made the country’s territory available for disposal by two foreign governments. In August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union were bargaining over an internationally recognized state and the lives of people who inhabited it. Berlin and Moscow also had a history of cooperation. The Treaty of Rapallo in 1922 restored relations between Weimar Germany and Soviet Russia and settled outstanding claims. The Berlin Treaty of 1926 continued the relationship and provided for neutrality under specified circumstances. Both governments had reasons to escape diplomatic isolation. Their accommodation demonstrated that ideological differences did not prevent cooperation where their interests met. [5] Hitler’s accession to power in 1933 fundamentally changed the character of German policy. Nazi hostility to communism was bound up with a racial vision of conquest. The idea of Lebensraum envisaged expansion into eastern Europe, German settlement and the displacement or subordination of peoples the regime considered inferior. It gave the German–Soviet confrontation an importance that went far beyond an ordinary disagreement between states. An agreement with Stalin could serve Hitler’s immediate purposes without ending those longer ambitions. [6] The sequence of German advances narrowed the room for compromise. Rearmament and the remilitarization of the Rhineland were followed by the annexation of Austria in March 1938. Later that year, the crisis over Czechoslovakia brought Britain and France to Munich. On 29–30 September, their leaders joined Germany and Italy in accepting the transfer of the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia was excluded from the conference that determined its territorial losses. [7] Munich also left the Soviet Union outside the negotiations. For Stalin, the episode gave further grounds to distrust Western willingness to resist Hitler. Yet the agreement failed even on the narrower promise that concessions would satisfy Germany. In March 1939, German forces occupied the Czech lands. The destruction of Czechoslovakia exposed ambitions extending beyond the incorporation of German-speaking populations. London and Paris faced a question they could no longer comfortably postpone: where would they resist the next demand? [8]

Poland between two powers

German pressure now centred on Poland. Hitler’s government wanted the Free City of Danzig, today Gdańsk, incorporated into Germany and sought an extraterritorial transport connection through the Polish Corridor. The language of roads and territorial adjustments understated the political stakes. Accepting German demands risked making Polish independence increasingly dependent on Berlin’s goodwill; refusing them exposed Poland to a stronger neighbour already willing to use force. Warsaw refused. On 31 March 1939, Britain publicly guaranteed Polish independence. France also stood behind Poland. The guarantee raised the prospective cost of a German attack, but a promise of support did not solve the military problem of how to deliver it. Britain and France lay to the west of Germany. The Soviet Union was the great power to the east, and its intentions mattered to every calculation about a European war. [9] German planning did not wait for an agreement with Moscow. On 3 April, Hitler issued instructions for Fall Weiss, the operation against Poland, with preparations allowing an attack from the beginning of September. On 28 April, he renounced Germany’s existing nonaggression arrangement with Poland. The sequence is essential: the August pact facilitated an aggressive policy that was already taking shape. It did not suddenly create Germany’s interest in attacking its neighbour. [9] [8] Poland’s difficulty was that Soviet assistance carried dangers of its own. Memories of the Polish–Soviet War were recent, and relations were burdened by territorial and political antagonisms. Permission for the Red Army to cross Polish territory would have required Warsaw to trust a government it regarded as a potential enemy. Refusal, on the other hand, made practical military cooperation against Germany extremely difficult. There was no simple way to reconcile these positions. Soviet planners wanted to know how their forces could reach a German enemy. Polish leaders wanted to know what would happen to their sovereignty if Soviet troops entered. Britain and France sought a deterrent strong enough to prevent war while lacking authority to promise another country’s territory as a military passage. The crisis joined an urgent strategic need to a profound absence of trust. [10] [11]

The diplomatic choice

During the 1930s, Soviet diplomacy had pursued collective security against aggression. Maxim Litvinov, the foreign commissar closely associated with cooperation with the Western powers, was replaced by Molotov on 3 May 1939. In retrospect, the appointment can look like the first decisive step towards the pact. Contemporaries did not agree about what it meant. American diplomatic reporting the next day recorded several interpretations. The Soviet ambassador in Paris denied a change of policy. Polish foreign minister Józef Beck reportedly expected a change of method more than direction. French assessments were also cautious. These reports do not reveal Stalin’s private intentions. They do show why the final agreement should not be read backwards into every earlier decision, as though its outcome had been certain throughout the spring. [12] By August, Britain, France and the Soviet Union were discussing military cooperation. The negotiations foundered in part on the transit question. A French assessment reported by Steinhardt on 23 August placed considerable blame on Polish refusal to accept Soviet military assistance. That was the French ambassador’s judgment, shaped by his own diplomatic position. It should not be mistaken for a complete explanation of the failure or proof that Poland was obliged to accept Soviet entry. [10] British reporting exposed the same difficulty from another direction. In discussions with Molotov, the British ambassador, Sir William Seeds, pointed out that London could not authorize Soviet passage through Poland or Romania without those countries’ agreement. Military necessity, political consent and national survival were being argued at the same time. The correspondence documents an impasse; it cannot, by itself, establish exactly when Stalin finally abandoned the Western option. [11] Germany could offer something very different. Instead of requiring agreement among states suspicious of one another, Berlin could bargain directly with Moscow over territories belonging to others. A German–Soviet understanding promised Stalin immediate freedom from a German attack, room for territorial expansion and time outside the opening phase of a European war. It promised Hitler relief from the danger that the Soviet Union would join a coalition against him when he attacked Poland. The prospective benefits were also asymmetric. Germany was preparing the immediate attack that would ignite the European war. The Soviet leadership was deciding how to position its state in relation to that attack and what it could obtain from agreement with Berlin. Their collaboration joined different projects; it did not require identical aims or a common view of the future. These were calculations of advantage made under uncertainty. Hitler still had to consider whether Britain and France would fight, while Stalin could not know the course of a Western war. Historians have consequently debated how far Soviet policy sought a temporary respite and how far it envisaged sustained cooperation with Germany. Geoffrey Roberts, discussing his research for *Stalin’s Wars*, described moving towards the view that Stalin contemplated a longer relationship, rather than treating it solely as a pause before an inevitable clash. That interpretation concerns the expected duration of cooperation; the documentary evidence of territorial bargaining is less ambiguous. The protocol makes a purely defensive explanation inadequate because Moscow was negotiating opportunities to expand its power over other states. Neither an interpretation based on security nor one emphasizing territorial ambition can turn those states’ absence from the negotiations into consent. [13] [2] Economic negotiations helped open the political door. A commercial agreement concluded on 19 August provided for a German credit of 200 million Reichsmarks for Soviet purchases of industrial goods, with repayment through raw-material deliveries. In a memorandum written ten days later, the German official Karl Schnurre described the negotiations as having renewed political contacts. The memorandum is retrospective, but it makes clear that the commercial and diplomatic approaches were connected. [14] On 20 August, Hitler sent Stalin a personal message accepting a Soviet draft of the nonaggression treaty and urging an immediate visit by Ribbentrop. He wanted the foreign minister received on 22 or 23 August, with full authority to settle both the treaty and an additional protocol. His accusations against Poland formed part of Germany’s diplomatic case, not an impartial account of the crisis. What the message establishes beyond doubt is the urgency: Hitler wanted a decision within days. [15] Stalin answered on 21 August, agreeing to receive Ribbentrop on the 23rd. His reply expressed the hope that the agreement would improve relations between the two states. Behind the conventional language lay a rapid transformation. While other governments were still trying to understand Moscow’s intentions, the German foreign minister was preparing to conclude a bargain at the highest level. [16]

A night in Moscow

Ribbentrop’s arrival did not mean every territorial question had been settled. The surviving German correspondence shows bargaining continuing into the evening. After an initial meeting lasting three hours with Stalin and Molotov, he reported a decisive Soviet demand concerning two Latvian ports. Moscow wanted Libau and Windau included in its sphere of influence. Ribbentrop sought Hitler’s approval. [17] The reply from Berlin was brief: “Answer is Yes. Agreed.” An archival annotation records its receipt in Moscow at 11 p.m. The exchange is unusually revealing because it reduces the abstract language of spheres to a specific negotiation over places. Latvia had not consented to this transaction. Its ports were being discussed as concessions one foreign government could make to another. [18] The conversation ranged much more widely than the wording of the treaty. A German memorandum recorded discussions of Britain, France, Italy, Turkey and Japan, along with the Anti-Comintern Pact directed against communist influence. The document also described ceremonial toasts, including one by Stalin to Hitler. Such details capture the public performance of a sudden accommodation, but their evidentiary limits matter: this is a German diplomatic account, not an independent verbatim transcript of everything said in the room. [19] The two regimes had found a way to suspend their immediate confrontation without resolving the ideological conflict between them. Each expected to gain from the other’s restraint. Each could present the resulting agreement as a contribution to peace, although both were discussing what might happen to their neighbours if the territorial order was overturned.

A detail in the cables

Two ports helped settle the bargain

Libau and Windau are the German names used in the diplomatic correspondence for modern Liepāja and Ventspils. Ribbentrop’s request and Berlin’s answer preserve a moment of last-minute bargaining over Latvia’s Baltic coast. The final secret protocol placed Latvia on the Soviet side of the agreed division of interests.

[17] [18] [2]

Two documents, two audiences

The public treaty contained seven articles. Germany and the Soviet Union undertook to refrain from violence and aggression against one another, to avoid supporting a third power engaged in hostilities against the other, and to remain in contact over matters of common interest. They promised peaceful settlement of disputes and agreed not to participate in groupings directed against the other party. Its projected duration was ten years, with an automatic extension of five years unless notice of termination was given in advance. Ratification was to follow, but the treaty entered into force immediately upon signature. The legal form suggested continuity and stability at precisely the moment when the strategic relationship had changed with extraordinary speed. [1] There was a consequential omission. The treaty contained no explicit provision releasing one party from its obligations if the other attacked a third country. British diplomats had raised this issue with Molotov while the agreement was being discussed. A promise of neutrality could therefore help an aggressor as readily as it could reassure a state fearing attack. The absence of such a qualification mattered to Poland more than the treaty’s language of peaceful relations. [11]

Made public

A nonaggression treaty

Promises governing relations between Germany and the Soviet Union. Ten-year term; effective on signature.

Kept secret

A division of interests

Proposed spheres across eastern Europe, negotiated without the affected states’ consent.

The secret protocol addressed those third countries directly. Under the formula of a possible “territorial and political rearrangement,” it divided German and Soviet interests across a broad region. Finland, Estonia and Latvia fell within the Soviet sphere. Lithuania was initially on the German side, with the northern Lithuanian frontier serving as the dividing line between the two spheres. The document also recognized Lithuania’s interest in the Vilna region, including the city then within Poland and now known as Vilnius. [2] For Poland, the protocol proposed an approximate division along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers. It left open whether an independent Polish state would survive and what its frontiers might be. Those questions were to be settled by subsequent agreement between Berlin and Moscow. The uncertainty was itself revealing: the signatories treated the continued existence of a neighbouring sovereign state as a matter for their own convenience. In southeastern Europe, the Soviet side emphasized its interest in Bessarabia, then part of Romania, while Germany declared political disinterest in that territory. The protocol thus extended well beyond Poland. It offered a framework in which German and Soviet ambitions could proceed without immediate conflict with each other. [2] Even the river names require careful reading. An approximate diplomatic division was not a surveyed frontier, and a sphere of influence was not an account of who controlled a town, road or bridge. Those are different kinds of historical information. Reading the August protocol alongside the later September treaty shows both continuity of purpose and the willingness of its makers to alter the territorial terms when circumstances changed. The text did not establish a timetable for invasions, supply a joint operational plan or transfer lawful sovereignty over the territories concerned. Nor did it draw the final occupation boundary in Poland. The distinction is indispensable to reading the atlas: an agreed sphere of influence on 23 August must not be coloured as if it were territory already conquered that day.

Names on the document

Stalin was present. He did not sign.

The signatures belonged to Molotov and Ribbentrop. Stalin’s presence and political authority were central to the negotiations, but his name was not one of the treaty’s signatures. The alternative name “Hitler–Stalin Pact” identifies the leaders responsible for the bargain; “Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact” identifies its signatories.

[1] [3]

What the world could see

The announcement transformed the diplomatic situation before most governments could discover the territorial terms. British reports recorded suspicion of a new partition, but suspicion was different from possession of the secret protocol. For London and Paris, the immediate problem was whether an agreement intended to isolate Poland would also discourage them from resisting Germany. For Warsaw, the danger was that the collapse of the hoped-for coalition would leave an alliance on paper without a practicable means of delivering help. [11] Britain’s response included making its commitment more formal. On 25 August, London and Warsaw signed their Agreement of Mutual Assistance. Its public text promised help if either party became involved in hostilities through aggression by a European power, and also addressed threats to independence that compelled armed resistance. This was a warning that a German–Soviet arrangement had not removed the prospect of British belligerency. It supplied no immediate solution to the geographical difficulty of assisting Poland. [20] Polish diplomacy, meanwhile, continued to present willingness to negotiate without surrendering independence. In his reply to President Franklin Roosevelt on 25 August, President Ignacy Mościcki said that Poland was ready for direct discussions and procedures of conciliation; he also emphasized that Poland was making no territorial demands. This was an official Polish representation of its position, intended to influence American and wider opinion. It matters because the surviving record includes an attempt to avert war alongside the preparations to resist it. Roosevelt’s appeal was diplomatic intervention by a country that had made no commitment to fight for Poland. [21] The alliance and Italy’s position temporarily complicated Hitler’s timetable. The postwar International Military Tribunal’s reconstruction, based on captured German documents, identified both the Anglo-Polish agreement and Mussolini’s unwillingness to enter an immediate war as factors in the postponement of the attack planned for 26 August. Daladier also appealed directly to Hitler on 26 August. These developments did not reverse German policy, but the postponement demonstrates that the decision in Moscow had not settled the decisions in London, Paris or Rome. Germany still faced a choice about accepting the risk of a wider war. [22] The agreement also unsettled Germany’s relationships farther afield. Japan, a partner in the Anti-Comintern Pact, was fighting Soviet forces at Khalkhin Gol, also known as Nomonhan, during the same summer. Tokyo’s struggle with Moscow gave the German reversal an immediate strategic meaning. A government associated with opposition to international communism had reached an accommodation with the Soviet Union while Japanese troops were engaged against it. [23] For the states mentioned in the secret protocol, the danger was more direct. Their security had become part of an arrangement they could neither inspect nor influence. The public treaty presented a relationship between two powers; the secret protocol disclosed the territorial price those powers were prepared to impose on others. That combination explains why the pact’s importance cannot be measured solely by whether Germany and the Soviet Union temporarily refrained from attacking one another.

The decision that remained

The pact changed the risks surrounding an invasion that Germany was already preparing. Hitler obtained Soviet nonaggression and a private accommodation over territory; Stalin obtained scope for expansion and cooperation with a Germany about to confront the Western powers. Their expectations need not have been identical for the bargain to facilitate aggression. The failure of the Western negotiations helps explain the available choices, but it does not remove responsibility for the choice made in Moscow. On 23 August, Poland still controlled its territory. The agreement supplied neither a final occupation boundary nor a joint operational timetable, and its promise of ten years’ nonaggression was a statement of intention whose durability remained untested. The immediate test was approaching elsewhere: whether Germany would invade Poland despite Britain’s renewed commitment and the risk that France would also fight. The [study of 1 September](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) follows that decision into the places where it had to be carried out—railway crossings, frontier positions and roads on which military advantage still had to be converted into victory. Reports establish what an official conveyed or believed, rather than providing unmediated access to Stalin’s intentions.
